WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Investigators with bomb-making components in their luggage and on their person were able to pass through security checkpoints at 19 U.S. airports without detection, according to the Government Accountability Office. Passengers pass through security at O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, Illinois. GAO officials are expected to testify about the investigation Thursday before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. The investigators reported that most of the time security officers followed Transportation Security Administration policies and procedures, but investigators were able to take advantage of "weaknesses in TSA procedures and other vulnerabilities." "These weaknesses were identified based on a review of public information," the planned GAO testimony says. Investigators concluded that if they had attempted the same test at other airports, they would have evaded detection. But the GAO did not detail the weaknesses because they "are sensitive security information." The investigators obtained the bomb-making components at local stores and over the Internet for less than $150, according to testimony.  Watch a tester point out a TSA mistake » . The GAO said its investigators also tested the devices that could be built with the components they smuggled and discovered that "a terrorist using these devices could cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers." The GAO investigators devised two types of devices: an "improvised explosive device" made of a liquid explosive and a low-yield detonator, and an "improvised incendiary device" that could be created by combining commonly available products prohibited in carry-on luggage. The GAO said it found the instructions for creating the devices "using publicly available information," including Internet searches. According to the testimony, a transportation security officer barred one of the investigators from bringing an unlabeled bottle of medicated shampoo through the checkpoint. But the security officer allowed a liquid component of the improvised explosive device to pass through undetected, although that item is prohibited by the TSA. In another test, the investigator put coins in his pockets to assure he would get a secondary inspection. But the officer, using a hand-wand and a pat-down, failed to detect any of the prohibited items the investigator was carrying. The GAO said it had briefed the TSA on its findings "to help them take corrective action." In testimony to be provided to the same congressional committee, TSA chief Kip Hawley defends the administration's policies and procedures, saying that the screening checkpoints are but one of a "multilayered approach to security." "We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer," according to the testimony. "Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts -- and together, they are formidable." Hawley sketches for members of Congress 19 security steps the TSA employs before, during and after checkpoint screening. "Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right," he says. "Linked together, they are effective and daunting." Although it would not discuss the specific nature of its recommendations, the GAO said it recommended establishing special screening lines based on risk and passengers with special needs. The TSA should introduce more "aggressive, visible and unpredictable" measures to detect concealed items and develop new technology for screening at checkpoints. Hawley's said the TSA concurs with the GAO's recommendations and specifically discussed several "new technology" items that he said were "greatly improving our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items." Among the new technology, he said, were whole body imagers, bottled liquids scanners, hand-held explosives scanners and advanced technology X-rays. And, he added, "our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today." He also said the TSA is constantly conducting covert tests of the screening process, including detection of prohibited liquids and IEDs. "The nation's aviation system remains secure," he said, "but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism."  E-mail to a friend .

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Undercover covert investigators carrying concealed bomb-making components successfully bypassed security checkpoints undetected at 19 U.S. airports—including Chicago’s O'Hare International Airport—according to a report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO). 

Officials from the GAO are scheduled to present these findings on Thursday in testimony before the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

According to the GAO's prepared testimony, while Transportation Security Administration (TSA) officers adhered to standard policies and procedures most of the time, undercover agents were still able to exploit "weaknesses in TSA procedures and other vulnerabilities." The report notes that these systemic flaws were identified primarily through a review of publicly available information. Investigators concluded that had they conducted similar tests at other domestic airports, they likewise would have evaded detection. The GAO withheld specific details regarding the security gaps, classifying them as "sensitive security information."

The report reveals that investigators purchased the necessary bomb-making materials at local retail stores and over the internet for less than $150. Video footage from the investigation highlights specific TSA oversights during the screening process. To test the viability of these smuggled components, the GAO assembled two types of devices: an improvised explosive device (IED) consisting of a liquid explosive with a low-yield detonator, and an improvised incendiary device fabricated from commonly available products prohibited in carry-on baggage. Instructions for crafting both devices were obtained entirely through open-source channels, including basic internet searches. 

Subsequent testing confirmed the potential lethality of the contraband. The GAO reported that "a terrorist using these devices could cause severe damage to an airplane and threaten the safety of passengers."

The testimony details notable inconsistencies in checkpoint enforcement. In one instance, a transportation security officer prohibited an investigator from bringing an unlabeled bottle of medicated shampoo through the checkpoint, yet allowed a liquid component of an improvised explosive device—also explicitly banned by the TSA—to pass through undetected. In another test, an investigator deliberately placed coins in his pockets to trigger a secondary screening; despite subjecting the investigator to a hand-wand scan and a pat-down, the screening officer failed to discover any of the concealed, prohibited items.

The GAO stated it has already briefed the TSA on these vulnerabilities to facilitate immediate corrective action. 

In companion testimony prepared for the same congressional panel, TSA Administrator Kip Hawley defended the agency’s protocols, emphasizing that checkpoint screeners represent just one component of a broader, "multilayered approach to security."

"We recognize that, despite our efforts to make each layer as strong as possible, a concerted effort may target any one layer," Hawley’s testimony reads. "Our ongoing success is a result of the tremendous power in the reinforced, multiple layers. Truly, the whole is greater than the sum of the parts—and together, they are formidable."

Hawley outlined for lawmakers the 19 distinct security measures deployed by the TSA before, during, and after checkpoint screenings. "Each and every one of these 19 security layers is important and strong in its own right," he stated. "Linked together, they are effective and daunting."

While the GAO declined to publicly disclose the precise nature of its classified recommendations, it confirmed recommending the implementation of specialized, risk-based screening lanes tailored for passengers with specific needs. The agency also advised the TSA to deploy more "aggressive, visible, and unpredictable" detection measures and to accelerate the development of advanced screening technologies.

Hawley reported that the TSA concurs with the GAO’s recommendations, highlighting several newly adopted technologies designed to "greatly improve our effectiveness in detecting prohibited items." These tools include whole-body imagers, bottled-liquid scanners, handheld explosives detectors, and advanced-technology X-ray systems. 

"Our pursuit of new technology is not limited to what I described today," Hawley added, noting that the TSA continuously conducts its own covert tests on screening procedures, specifically targeting concealed liquids and IEDs. 

"The nation's aviation system remains secure," Hawley concluded, "but requires ongoing improvement and vigilance to stay ahead of the threat of terrorism."

**GAO Report Reveals Critical Security Vulnerabilities at TSA Airport Checkpoints**

**WASHINGTON** — A damning new report by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) has uncovered major security gaps at Transportation Security Administration (TSA) airport checkpoints across the nation, raising fresh concerns about passenger safety and the effectiveness of current screening protocols.

According to the nonpartisan congressional watchdog agency’s report, published Thursday, undercover covert testing revealed high failure rates in detecting prohibited items, including mock weapons and simulated explosives, at dozens of major U.S. airports over the past year. 

The GAO attributed the systemic vulnerabilities to a combination of aging technology, inadequate screener training, operational fatigue, and high staff turnover among Transportation Security Officers (TSOs). 

"While TSA has made incremental progress in deploying new detection technologies, significant operational blind spots remain," the report stated. "In covert testing, screeners repeatedly failed to identify threat objects concealed on passengers and in carry-on baggage, pointing to widespread procedural and technological deficiencies."

While specific failure rates and test methodologies remain classified for national security reasons, officials familiar with the findings described the outcome of the covert tests as "deeply troubling," noting that failure rates in certain categories mirrored gaps identified in previous audits over the past decade.

Key findings in the GAO report include:

* **Technology Delays:** Slow rollout of advanced Computed Tomography (CT) bag scanners and credential authentication technology, leaving many busiest airports reliant on outdated 2D X-ray machines.
* **Training Gaps:** Inconsistent recurring training for checkpoint screeners, leading to varied detection standards across different regional hubs.
* **Staffing Strain:** Persistent understaffing and high turnover rates, which investigators noted increase fatigue and reduce vigilance during peak travel hours.
* **Oversight Deficiencies:** A lack of standardized supervisor audits to ensure screeners strictly adhere to standard operating procedures.

The findings sparked immediate reaction from Capitol Hill, where lawmakers expressed frustration over the agency's repeated failure to eliminate long-standing screening weaknesses.

"Taxpayers spend billions of dollars every year on aviation security, yet this report shows alarming lapses at the front lines of our defense," said Rep. Mark Green (R-TN), Chairman of the House Homeland Security Committee, in a statement. "The TSA must immediately address these vulnerability gaps. Passengers deserve to know that the checkpoints they pass through are effectively detecting real-world threats."

In a formal response appended to the report, TSA leadership accepted all eight recommendations made by the GAO. The agency emphasized that physical checkpoint screening is only one layer of a broader, multi-tiered security system that includes intelligence gathering, air marshals, canine teams, and hardened cockpit doors.

"TSA screens more than 2.5 million passengers daily, and our commitment to security is absolute," a TSA spokesperson said Thursday. "While any failure in covert testing is unacceptable, we treat these findings as critical learning opportunities. We are actively accelerating the procurement of next-generation CT technology, enhancing our recurrent training modules, and addressing workforce retention."

The GAO recommended that the TSA establish a clear timeline for replacing legacy equipment, overhaul its screener recertification programs, and implement stricter oversight mechanisms for checkpoint performance. 

The House Homeland Security Committee is expected to call TSA leadership to testify on the report's findings in a public hearing next month.

**CAPITOL HILL SHOCKED: Undercover Agents Smuggle Liquid Explosive Components Past TSA Screeners**

**By Alex Mercer**  
**WASHINGTON** — In a chilling revelation that has sent shockwaves through Capitol Hill, federal investigators revealed Thursday that covert government agents successfully smuggled components for liquid explosives and detonators past Transportation Security Administration (TSA) screeners at major airports across the country, exposing severe vulnerabilities in the nation’s aviation security network.

According to a report presented to Congress by the Government Accountability Office (GAO), undercover auditors achieved a 100 percent success rate during secret testing conducted at 19 major U.S. airports earlier this year. Investigators were able to purchase common household products at ordinary retail stores for under $100, conceal them on their bodies and in carry-on bags, and walk through primary security checkpoints completely undetected. Once past security, the components could have been combined in an aircraft lavatory to assemble a viable Improvised Explosive Device (IED).

The findings are particularly alarming given that they come just over a year after the TSA introduced strict liquid restrictions following the disrupted 2006 transatlantic aircraft plot in the United Kingdom. 

"The security rules were clearly violated, but more importantly, our tests show that the system remains vulnerable," testified Gregory D. Kutz, Managing Director of Forensic Audits and Special Investigations at the GAO, during a tense hearing before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. 

Addressing a panel of visibly frustrated lawmakers, Kutz described how easily auditors bypassed physical and technological safeguards. 

"Our investigators concealed these items on their bodies and in their carry-on luggage," Kutz told the committee. "In every single test, at every airport we visited, our agents walked right past TSA screeners without being stopped or challenged. The liquid explosive components were not detected by the X-ray machines, and the hidden detonator components were not discovered during magnetometer screening or secondary checks."

Lawmakers expressed outrage over the findings, questioning the effectiveness of the billions of dollars invested in the TSA since the terror attacks of September 11, 2001.

"This is a deeply disturbing report that should alarm every traveling American," said Committee Chairman Sen. Joseph Lieberman (I-CT). "The fact that undercover agents could assemble the components of a lethal bomb from materials bought at local convenience stores, walk through TSA checkpoints undetected, and board a plane is simply unacceptable. Senator Susan Collins (R-ME), the committee’s ranking member, echoed Lieberman’s frustration, pointing out the disconnect between passenger hassle and actual security outcomes. "Passengers are taking off their shoes, dumping their water bottles, and waiting in line for hours under the impression that these measures are keeping them safe," Collins said. Appearing before the committee to defend the agency, TSA Administrator Kip Hawley acknowledged the audit's troubling outcomes but urged lawmakers and the public to look at the broader defense system.

"We do not rely on any single layer of security to protect the aviation system," Hawley testified. "While checkpoint screening is a critical component, it is just one of more than twenty layers of security—ranging from intelligence gathering and air marshals to hardened cockpit doors and vigilant passengers—that safeguard flights every day."

Hawley assured the committee that the TSA would immediately use the GAO’s findings to alter screening protocols, retrain checkpoint personnel, and accelerate the deployment of advanced technology, such as whole-body imaging scanners and advanced X-ray units designed to better detect liquid threats.

"We take these covert tests very seriously," Hawley added. "They show us where our vulnerabilities are so we can close them before a real adversary tries to exploit them."

However, GAO officials warned that technology alone will not solve the problem without improvements in screener training and adherence to standard procedures. Kutz noted that in several instances, screeners failed to follow basic TSA protocols, such as performing proper pat-downs when walk-through metal detectors alarmed or properly inspecting carry-on items that appeared suspicious on X-ray monitors.

As the nation approaches the busy holiday travel season, the GAO report leaves aviation experts and the public questioning whether the current security apparatus provides genuine safety or merely the illusion of it.
